cards.front: What does it mean for an integer type to be unsigned?
cards.back: Every bit pattern is a non-negative number: range 0 … 2ⁿ−1
cards.extra: An unsigned type has no sign bit, so the same 32 bits that would mean -1 as a signed int mean 4294967295. You lose negatives and gain twice the positive range.

cards.front: Java's byte, short, int and long are signed. Which primitive is the unsigned one?
cards.extra: There is no unsigned int in Java. char is the only primitive whose value range starts at zero and has no negatives, because it holds a UTF-16 code unit.

cards.front: What is the range of a signed 32-bit int?
cards.extra: Two's complement gives one more negative value than positive: −2147483648 to 2147483647. The asymmetry is why Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) stays negative.

cards.front: Those same 32 bits read as unsigned would cover which range?
cards.extra: The bit count is unchanged; only the interpretation changes. That is why unsigned arithmetic is usually about reading and comparing, not about a separate type.
0xFF is 255, which is above Byte.MAX_VALUE (127), so the cast keeps the low 8 bits and 0b11111111 reads as −1 in two's complement. Reading it back as unsigned needs Byte.toUnsignedInt(b).

cards.text: byte b = -1; widened to int gives {{c1::−1}}, not 255, because widening performs {{c2::sign extension}}.
cards.extra: The sign bit is copied into the new high bits. To get 255 you must mask: b & 0xFF.

cards.text: >> is an {{c1::arithmetic}} shift that copies the sign bit; >>> is a {{c2::logical}} shift that fills with zeros.
cards.extra: So -8 >> 1 is −4, while -8 >>> 1 is 2147483644 — the second one treats the value as unsigned.

cards.back: Two's complement wraparound — Java integer arithmetic overflows silently
cards.extra: Adding 1 to 0b0111…1 carries into the sign bit. No exception, no warning: the result is just negative. This is the classic bug behind reversed comparisons and wrong totals.

cards.front: Which Math methods throw instead of wrapping on overflow?
cards.extra: They throw ArithmeticException when the result does not fit. Math.addExact(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1) fails loudly where + would silently produce Integer.MIN_VALUE.

cards.text: To treat an int as unsigned, Java puts static helpers on {{c1::Integer}} — e.g. {{c2::parseUnsignedInt}}, toUnsignedString, compareUnsigned.
cards.extra: The bits never change; only the interpretation does. Integer.toUnsignedString(-1) returns "4294967295", and Integer.compareUnsigned(-1, 1) says -1 is greater.
